946.title: Cairo founded
946.hook: the Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, found a new city beside the Nile
946.howItsDone: Isma'ili Muslims today count the Fatimid imams as part of their own history, and Cairo's Fatimid gates and mosques are still visited and prayed in.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Qarawiyyin, the mosque in Fez that Fatimah al-Fihri built with her inheritance, where a university grew. Your line was: she founded a university.

Ropes are strung around a plain beside the Nile, hung with bells. Workers wait with their tools. Astrologers watch the sky for the right moment to begin, when they'll shake the ropes and the digging will start. Then a crow lands on a rope. The bells ring. The workers dig. And the planet rising at that moment, so the story goes, was the one Arabic astronomers called the victorious. That, people say, is how the city got its name: al-Qahira. In English, Cairo.

Take the crow as a story people tell; the history behind it is sturdier. The Fatimids named themselves for Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and wife of Ali, and they claimed descent from her. They were Isma'ili Shi'i Muslims. Shi'i Muslims hold that leadership of the community passed to Ali, and then to imams among his and Fatimah's descendants. The Isma'ilis followed one line of those imams, and the Fatimid caliphs said they were those imams. That made a crowded sky of caliphs: one in Baghdad, a Fatimid caliph who had already claimed the title in North Africa, and the Cordoba caliph you met last week, who took it after them. Sunnis and Shi'is understood that leadership differently, and still do. The Fatimids rose in North Africa, then took Egypt. Their general, Jawhar, laid out a new walled city for his caliph, al-Mu'izz. An older city, Fustat, already stood nearby, built in the early years of Muslim rule in Egypt. The new city was a royal enclosure: palaces, a great mosque, walls with gates. Much of ordinary life went on outside it, in Fustat. Over the years the two grew into each other, until the name Cairo covered both. Today Isma'ili Muslims around the world count the Fatimid imams as part of their own story, and Cairo still keeps Fatimid gates and mosques. A city built to announce a claim, then lived in by everyone. The victorious city.

segments.voice: Picture the Nile running north, and on its east bank two cities side by side, an old busy one and a new walled one with palaces, slowly merging. Now picture your own town the same way: where was the old center, where did newer neighborhoods grow, and who lives in them? If you pray, remember the people of your city; if you don't, hold them in mind with good will.
Cairo founded. The Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, built a royal city beside the old Fustat, and named it al-Qahira, the victorious. Today's word.
Your line: the victorious city. Fatimid gates still stand among its streets. That's day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Al-Azhar in Cairo
947.hook: the mosque and university founded by the Fatimids, later a great center of Sunni learning
947.howItsDone: Al-Azhar is still a working mosque and a place of Islamic learning in Cairo, and students study the Qur'an, hadith, law and Arabic there, some in circles around a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cairo founded. The Fatimids built a royal city beside the Nile and called it al-Qahira. Your line was: the victorious city.

A student sits on a mat with his back against a stone column. A teacher sits against the next column over, a small ring of students around him. Another ring sits by the next pillar, and another by the one after that. Nobody has a desk. Some have a book on their knees, some only their memory. That's a class in this mosque: a circle on the floor, beside a pillar. The new city by the Nile needed a great mosque, and its builders raised one close to the palaces: al-Azhar.
screen: `A RING OF STUDENTS BY A PILLAR.` → `NO DESKS, JUST A MAT.` → `A GREAT MOSQUE FOR A NEW CITY.`

segments.voice: Al-Azhar was built by the Fatimids, the Isma'ili dynasty from yesterday. Tradition explains the name as the radiant, or the shining one, and some connect it with Fatimah al-Zahra, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, from whom the Fatimids traced their line. Scholars give that link with a little caution, and so will i. At first it taught the Isma'ili teaching of its founders. Later, when the Fatimid age ended and new rulers held Egypt, the mosque came to teach Sunni learning, and became one of the places Sunni students traveled toward: the Qur'an, hadith, law, Arabic grammar, the sciences that serve the text. One building, two chapters of Islamic history, neither one ranked. Why travel so far to sit on a mat by a pillar? The Qur'an has a short prayer for that kind of hunger, one it teaches the Prophet to say. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Not wealth, not fame. Knowledge. Learning happened in a mosque, between the prayers; a class could stop for the call to prayer and pick up again after. And the method was the circle. A teacher read, explained and answered. Students copied, memorized, questioned, and when a teacher judged a student ready, gave permission to teach in turn. People today speak of al-Azhar as a thousand years of study. Whatever the exact count, the picture holds: someone, by a pillar, reading.

Hold the question, not the answer: what exactly don't you know? If you pray, you can say the line the Qur'an teaches, My Lord! Increase me in knowledge; if you don't, let the question sit quietly.

948.title: Ibn Tulun's mosque
948.hook: an old Cairo mosque with a spiral minaret
948.howItsDone: The mosque of Ibn Tulun still stands in Cairo, and visitors can climb the stair on the outside of its minaret. Dhikr is practiced by repeating short phrases such as Subhan Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Azhar in Cairo, where classes met in rings beside the pillars. Your line was: a thousand years of study.

Build the minaret like this. The man saying it holds up a strip of paper he's been idly rolling around his finger during a meeting, now a tight coil. That's a story told about Ahmad ibn Tulun, who governed Egypt in the name of the Abbasid caliphs before Cairo itself existed. It may not be true. But walk around his mosque today and the minaret does look a little like that coil: a stair wrapped around the outside of the tower, climbing as it turns.
screen: `A STRIP OF PAPER, ROLLED UP.` → `BUILD THE MINARET LIKE THIS.` → `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.`

segments.voice: Ibn Tulun built in his own capital, a settlement just south of where the Fatimids would later lay out Cairo. Over time the city grew around his mosque, so it now stands inside Cairo, older than the city around it. Step through the gate and the first thing is space: a huge open courtyard, plain arcades of pointed arches on every side, and a fountain in the middle for washing before prayer. Some visitors say the plainness is the point: nothing much to look at except light, shadow and the next arch. Then the stair. This minaret doesn't hide its steps inside. It puts them outside, so anyone looking up can see the path the caller to prayer would climb, turning and rising. Historians link the shape to the great spiral minaret at Samarra, the Abbasid capital where, tradition says, Ibn Tulun grew up. So the paper story and the Samarra story might both explain the same thing. A turning stair is also a good picture of remembrance, dhikr. You go around and around, every turn almost like the last, but higher each time. The Qur'an says it this way, in Pickthall's translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" In that picture, repeating the same words, the same prayers, the same small acts, isn't walking in a circle. It's climbing. The spiral stair.

segments.voice: If there are stairs near you, climb them as slowly as you can, one step at a time; if not, sit and let your attention go round with the breath, in, out, and again. If you pray, say a word of dhikr with each step or breath, such as Subhan Allah, glory be to God; if you don't, count them. Notice that every turn feels the same, and that you are not where you started.
Ibn Tulun. The governor of Egypt whose mosque, now inside Cairo, has a wide courtyard and a minaret whose stair winds around the outside. Today's word.
Your line: the spiral stair. Saying the same words again can be a way up. See you tomorrow.

949.title: The Nizamiyya colleges
949.hook: the vizier Nizam al-Mulk founds colleges across the east, where al-Ghazali taught
949.howItsDone: Madrasahs today range from children's Qur'an classes to colleges of Islamic law and theology, and some are supported by endowments (waqf) and gifts from their communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Tulun's mosque, with a stair that winds around the outside of its minaret. Your line was: the spiral stair.

Nothing comes out. A famous professor stands up to lecture in Baghdad, and he cannot speak. His tongue simply won't move. He tries again on other days; the words won't come. He can barely eat. The doctors say the trouble started in his heart, and no medicine of theirs will reach it. That professor was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, and he tells this story himself, in a short book about his search for certainty. His prized teaching chair was at a college in Baghdad called the Nizamiyya. Today's word is the kind of school it was: madrasah.
screen: `A PROFESSOR WHO CAN'T SPEAK.` → `AL-GHAZALI TELLS IT HIMSELF.` → `A COLLEGE IN BAGHDAD.`

segments.voice: Madrasah is simply the Arabic for a place of study, a school. In everyday Arabic it can still mean the school a child walks to in the morning. But in Islamic history it also names something particular: a college, with a building, teachers paid to teach, students given a room and food, the whole thing supported by a waqf, an endowment set aside for good. Nizam al-Mulk was a Persian vizier, the chief minister of the Seljuk sultans. He set up colleges in Baghdad and in other cities of the eastern lands, and they carried his name: the Nizamiyya. A student who could recite and understand could find a place to live and a teacher, paid for by the endowment rather than by his own family. That's where today's line comes from, a college in every city: a picture, not a count. Al-Ghazali was one of its great teachers. Then, by his own account, he walked away. He left the chair, the students and the reputation, and set out to travel and to practice what he had been teaching. Later he did teach again. In his telling, books had taught him what the Sufis said about the path, but walking it was something no book could do for him. So he left the college for the road. And some of the books he wrote after leaving are still studied in madrasahs.

950.title: Ibn Battuta
950.hook: the traveler from Tangier who set out for Mecca and kept going
950.howItsDone: Ibn Battuta's Rihla is read today as a travel book and a window on the Muslim world of his time, and pilgrims still set out for Mecca to perform the Hajj.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the madrasah, Nizam al-Mulk's endowed colleges, and al-Ghazali leaving his chair in Baghdad. Your line was: a college in every city.

Tangier, on the northern tip of Morocco. A young man is leaving it for Mecca, to make the pilgrimage. In his own telling, he goes alone, with no companion and no caravan to join, and parting from his parents weighs on him, and on them. He's a student of law. He plans to come home. Instead, the road keeps opening: Egypt, Syria, Mecca, then east and south and east again, for years, until his book reads like a map of a great stretch of the Muslim world of his time, and some lands beyond it. His name: Ibn Battuta.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN LEAVES TANGIER.` → `ALONE, FOR MECCA.` → `THE ROAD KEEPS OPENING.`

segments.voice: His book is called the Rihla, which simply means the journey. He didn't write it with his own pen. Home at last in Morocco, he told his story aloud, and a court scholar named Ibn Juzayy wrote it down and polished it. So what we read is a traveler's memory, shaped by an editor. Historians have questioned some passages, wondering whether he really reached every place he describes. That's worth knowing; the book is still a marvel. What kept him moving? Partly the pilgrimage. Partly that a man trained in Islamic law could find work almost anywhere the law was used. In one land he serves as a judge. In another he's a guest of a sultan, then out of favor, then on the road again. He prays in mosques he's never seen, eats at the tables of strangers, stays in lodges kept by Sufis for travelers. The world he walks through shares a language of prayer, a law and a habit of hospitality, even when everything else changes. One verse of the Qur'an tells its hearers to go and look. In Pickthall's translation: "Travel in the land and see how He originated creation." For Ibn Battuta the journey was not only distance. It was attention: to food, to customs, to scholars, to the strangeness and sameness of people. Much of what he described was other people: what they ate, how they prayed, how they treated a stranger at the door. The traveler.

951.title: Ibn Khaldun
951.hook: the historian of Tunis who studied how societies rise and fall
951.howItsDone: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah is read today by historians, sociologists and students of Islamic thought, and its idea of asabiyya, group feeling, is still discussed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Battuta, who set out from Tangier for Mecca and kept going. Your line was: the traveler.

Damascus is under siege. Outside the walls is the army of Timur, the conqueror. Inside, a scholar from North Africa decides he wants to meet the man himself. The gates are closed, so his friends lower him down the city wall on ropes. He walks into the conqueror's camp, is received, and the two talk about history, about kings, about the lands of the west. The scholar tells this himself, in the account of his own life. He was Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis, and he had spent years thinking about exactly this: why some peoples rise and conquer, and why their cities, in time, fall.
screen: `DAMASCUS UNDER SIEGE.` → `LOWERED DOWN THE WALL ON ROPES.` → `A SCHOLAR MEETS A CONQUEROR.`

segments.voice: Ibn Khaldun served sultans across North Africa and al-Andalus, fell in and out of favor, spent time in prison, and finally withdrew to a quiet fortress to write. He began with an introduction to a history of the world, and the introduction took on a life of its own: the Muqaddimah, the introduction. His big idea has an Arabic name, asabiyya. Group feeling: the bond that holds a people together, the loyalty that makes them stand by each other. He saw it strongest among people living hard lives in the desert and the mountains, where nobody survives alone. That bond, he argued, lets a group win power and build a state. Then comes the city. Comfort: fine clothes, soft beds, servants. Each generation inherits the power without the hardship that made it, and the bond quietly loosens. Rulers lean on paid soldiers instead of loyal kin. And one day a new group, with strong bonds and nothing to lose, comes in from the edge. He was writing about dynasties, but the question travels: anyone can ask it of a family, a team or a mosque community. The Qur'an has a line some readers set beside his idea. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts." Ibn Khaldun wrote as a believing Muslim and a judge. For him, studying how societies rise and fall was a way of reading the world with open eyes. Bonds build, luxury loosens.

Don't blame anyone; just notice, and think of one person in it you've drifted from. If you pray, hold that group before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

952.title: The Almoravids and Almohads
952.hook: reforming movements from the Sahara and the Atlas that ruled North Africa and Spain
952.howItsDone: The Almoravids and Almohads are remembered in North Africa through cities and buildings such as Marrakesh, and through the Maliki law and the teaching of tawhid that each emphasized.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Khaldun, and his idea that hardship binds a people and comfort loosens them. Your line was: bonds build, luxury loosens.

Ibn Khaldun wrote the history of two movements from his own corner of the world. First, out of the Sahara: a preacher among desert tribes, men who veil their faces, a small band devoted to prayer and strict living. In time they rule from the desert to al-Andalus. Then, out of the Atlas Mountains: another preacher, another band, sure the rulers have gone soft, who sweep down and replace them. Two waves of renewal, each coming in from the edge, each with the same promise: we'll bring things back to how they should be.
screen: `OUT OF THE SAHARA.` → `OUT OF THE ATLAS MOUNTAINS.` → `TWO WAVES OF RENEWAL.`

segments.voice: The Almoravids, in Arabic al-Murabitun, began with a teacher named Abd Allah ibn Yasin preaching among the Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara. Tradition ties the name to the ribat, a fortified retreat where people lived for prayer and for defense. Their strength was discipline and the Maliki law, followed closely. They founded Marrakesh, and under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they crossed the sea when Muslim rulers in al-Andalus, under pressure from Christian kingdoms to the north, asked for help. The Almohads, al-Muwahhidun, took a name meaning those who affirm the oneness of God, tawhid. Their founder, Ibn Tumart, preached in the Atlas that the Almoravids had grown too fond of law books and too lax in faith. His followers took Marrakesh and became the new rulers of North Africa and al-Andalus. Under them, Ibn Rushd, whom you met earlier, served as a judge and physician. The honest part: both movements began as calls to renewal, and both were strict. The Almohad years were hard for Jews and Christians in their lands, and some families left. And both, in their turn, softened, divided and were replaced. Ibn Khaldun saw his pattern in it. The Qur'an speaks of a community that calls others to good. In Pickthall's translation: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." A movement can take a verse like that as its calling. Ibn Khaldun's history asks what comes after: whether the bond that carried a movement to power holds once it is there.
screen: `AL-MURABITUN — THE PEOPLE OF THE RIBAT.` · `AL-MUWAHHIDUN — THE ONENESS OF GOD.` · `STRICT, AND HARD ON OTHERS.` · `EACH SOFTENS AND IS REPLACED.` · then, large: `RENEWAL FROM THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that has grown soft or careless and needs renewing: a habit, a promise, a prayer you've let slide. Then ask a second question: could you renew it without turning hard on the people around you? If you pray, ask for renewal with humility; if you don't, choose one small thing to begin again.
Tawhid. The affirming of God's oneness that named the Almohads, one of two reforming movements, with the Almoravids, that ruled North Africa and al-Andalus in turn. Today's word.
Your line: renewal from the desert. That closes a week of Cairo, al-Azhar, Ibn Tulun's stair, the madrasah, the traveler and Ibn Khaldun. Day nine hundred fifty-two.
